item.title: Please sell your Xbox Series X to Best Buy, asks Microsoft
item.itunes:title: Please sell your Xbox Series X to Best Buy, asks Microsoft
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Microsoft emails inactive Xbox Series X owners urging Best Buy trade-ins for up to $375 in gift cards
  • Amount is 'up to' $375, so actual trade value may be lower compared with $799 new price
  • Likely move to reclaim idle consoles for resale as production costs and RAM shortages drive supply issues

How long has it been since you used your Xbox Series X? If it's been a while, Microsoft would really like it if you'd sell it to Best Buy. The company has been sending out emails to people who haven't booted up their console in a while, asking them if they'd like to trade it in at their local Best Buy for up to $375 in gift cards.

Microsoft asks people with dormant Xbox Series Xs to think about selling it, please

It's likely a move to get more consoles to people who want one

As spotted by Notebook Check, people who own an Xbox Series X but haven't turned it on in a few months are reporting getting an email from Microsoft itself. The email is pretty clear: if your console is sitting around and collecting dust, you can hand it over at Best Buy and score up to $375 in gift cards.

That's just shy of half the price of a new Xbox Series X, which clocks in at $799 right now. Of course, that's the 'up to' price, so the actual amount you'd get when you trade in your console may be lower.

So, why is Microsoft advertising this? The company didn't reveal why, but in my opinion, it's likely Microsoft's bid to inject more consoles into the market. Given how production costs have skyrocketed due to the RAM crisis, I can imagine Microsoft wanting to encourage people with idle consoles to sell them, so that people who actually want to use them can get one.

Xbox officially unveils a way to digitize your physical game collection

The feature will launch for Xbox insiders first on August 31st.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: Most Event Viewer errors are normal, and you probably shouldn't be looking at them in the first place
item.itunes:title: Most Event Viewer errors are normal, and you probably shouldn't be looking at them in the first place
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever you run into problems with Windows 11, it's usually time to start diving into all the possible causes. One of the ways to do that, and one we've recommended quite often here at XDA, is to use Event Viewer to find possible errors that led to a crash or blue screen.

But digging through Event Viewer can be a scary experience. Not because it's confusing or complicated necessarily, but because it will show you a lot of errors that will make you think something is wrong, even if your PC is functioning exactly as expected.

Event Viewer errors have tiers

They're not all the same

When you open Event Viewer, you'll see a long list of messages with a few different types, mostly falling under Information, Warning, Error, or Critical categories. Information messages are the ones you'll most likely overlook, especially as they're also the most frequent type of message and just indicate that a specific thing has happened on the system. It usually means that the task was completed successfully.

You might be tempted to pour over all the other kinds of messages, but generally, there's not much of a reason to. With warning messages, they usually just indicate that a configuration or program could cause an error at some point, or that some configuration should be changed or checked for safety. Most of the time, there's nothing you really need or want to change.

Even the error messages don't necessarily have to mean anything big. Event Viewer logs pretty much everything that's happening on your computer — every attempt to connect to a service or the internet, or to load a file or program. A lot of the time, these things can fil on a first attempt for any number of reasons, and then function exactly as expected on a subsequent attempt, all without it ever being brought up to you during normal use.

I stopped opening Event Viewer after finding this buried Windows tool that actually makes sense

No more opening Event Viewer and immediately regretting it.

2
By  Korbin Brown

As of writing this, my laptop indicates there were 64 error messages and 108 warning messages in the last 24 hours, yet I've had no issues whatsoever. Of course, that's not to say Error messages are never important, but unless you're seeing an actual problem that ties into it. Failures and retries are natural parts of how your PC operates, and unless you know something is getting in the way of your work, there's no reason to lose sleep to peer through every error message in Event Viewer.

Critical errors are (usually) more important

You'll know when these happen

The one kind of message you probably shouldn't ignore when looking at Event Viewer is whatever falls under the Critical category, and the name is fairly self-explanatory. These errors indicate that the system encountered an error so severe that it caused a program or service to crash or close.

Many times, you'll see this error because your entire system crashed due to a Windows component failing, resulting in a blue screen of death. Whenever you see one of these screens, you can actually see an error message that tells you what to look for in Event Viewer, and that's where you can find more information about what actually caused it so you can find potential solutions.

5 built-in tools to use when troubleshooting Windows problems

You don't need third-party tools

2
By  Anurag Singh

Still, critical errors are also not always indicative of larger problems with your PC. Sometimes, your computer may simply shut down unexpectedly for reasons unrelated to the OS, and that would be marked as a Critical error because something caused the computer to shut down, but it wouldn't have to mean anything is wrong with the system. You can even cause one yourself by using a command such as taskkill /IM svchost.exe /f in your terminal (this will shut down your computer, so save your work beforehand).

It's a troubleshooting tool, not a maintenance system

Use it when you need it

The best way to look at it is that Event Viewer is more of a troubleshooting tool than a way to monitor your system regularly. You should look at the logs in Event Viewer when you're running into concrete problems. Going into Event Viewer and looking for the right timestamp and message can help you figure whether something is truly wrong with your system or not.

That could be because of a blue screen or application crash, but there are other application errors that could end up there, so it's always worth a look to see if you can spot the cause and eventually find a solution.

5 easy PC maintenance tasks that keep your system running like new

They're quick, easy, and ensure your PC feels like new for longer

2
By  Tanveer Singh

But if you're just doing a regular checkup to make sure everything is running as intended, there's no use in jumping the shark just because you see dozens of error messages in Event Viewer. Ultimately, it's there to help you diagnose a problem you already have, not to help you find new ones.

There may be better alternatives, too

Event Viewer makes things more stressful than they need to be

If you want to keep an eye on your PC's reliability and make sure things are running smoothly, there are other tools in Windows 11 that may do a better job of this than Event Viewer. One is Reliability Monitor, which organizes error and information messages more neatly into an overview that makes it easier to understand what's been happening on your PC. The information is essentially the same, but it's presented in a much clearer way.

Meanwhile, troubleshooting BSODs can be made easier with a program called BlueScreenView, which focuses just on the errors that caused blue screens and, again, provides a less daunting interface to look at them.

What really causes a Blue Screen of Death (BSOD)?

Here's how to find out

By  João Carrasqueira

Otherwise, if you want to keep your system running smoothly, there are other places you might want to look to help improve performance or make sure you're not piling up unnecessary files and apps. Check Task Manager for unnecessary startup apps, look through your app list for anything you might not need anymore, and run malware checks somewhat regularly. I always recommend MalwareBytes as the best way to detect all kinds of malware, though there are other great options.

item.title: This $100 Asus Windows laptop might be just what you're looking for
item.itunes:title: This $100 Asus Windows laptop might be just what you're looking for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The ASUS L410 laptop isn't going to be for everyone. However, if you need something super simple that's just for the basics, this laptop might be what you're looking for. It has a retail price of $250, but can now be had for just $100 when you buy it directly from ASUS. We don't know about you, but with that kind of discount, it's worth taking a look.

It'll be good for someone

If you can, we always recommend buying a laptop with more power than you need. However, we also understand that not everyone has the same budget. If you just need something that's going to work, the ASUS L410 laptop is going to be a prime choice.

You're looking at a laptop that's powered by an Intel Celeron N4020 chip that's paired with 4GB of RAM and 64GB of eMMC storage. It has a 14-inch 1080p screen, along with a backlit keyboard and touchpad.

For ports, it includes two USB-A ports, one USB-C port, HDMI, and a 3.5mm headphone jack. It has a VGA webcam, and the battery can last up to 12 hours. Again, not a bad combination here.

The $100 model comes with Windows 10 Home S, and for $50 more, you can grab one with Windows 11 Home S. To get this discount, you'll need to buy it directly from ASUS.

We aren't seeing this laptop priced like this anywhere else, so supplies could be short. Plus, the next alternative will be a Chromebook. If Windows laptop on a budget is a must, then get this while you still can.

item.title: People are now vibe-coding their smart TVs to strip them of ads and unwanted features
item.itunes:title: People are now vibe-coding their smart TVs to strip them of ads and unwanted features
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Vibe coders use LLMs to strip smart TVs down to just the apps, HDMI, and no ads or tracking.
  • Open GitHub projects like CleanYourTV and DumbTV automate reversible TV de-bloating via ADB, no root.
  • LLM reverse-engineering now ports and recreates software and hardware features, sidestepping corporate limits.

AI is getting so powerful that users are taking products into their own hands. Recently, we reported on how a team recreated Adobe's products using AI and offered them for free. Now, we're getting reports that people are vibe-coding solutions that strip the "smart" out of smart TVs, leaving them with just the bits people actually want.

A new wave of "dumb TV" vibe-coded apps are making their way online

People are even doing the job themselves

As spotted by TechCrunch, vibe coders have discovered that if you point a powerful LLM such as Claude at a smart TV, it can do a pretty good job of removing all the parts of it that you don't want. TechCrunch points at two GitHub projects that claim to do just that: CleanYourTV and DumbTV.

For a general idea of what these apps can do, here's the intro to DumbTV:

"Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for. dumbtv applies that over ADB from another machine — no root, nothing written to /system, every step reversible with one script."

These scripts have been made possible due to the increasing power of LLM coding, specifically, reverse-engineering. Over on the gaming side of XDA, we're reporting on people using AI to decompile and port games over to PC and other consoles, the most recent report being Pokémon: Let's Go arriving on PC. Combine that with the Adobe alternatives we mentioned earlier and this smart TV hack, and it seems people are beginning to use AI to modify products as they please, much to the chagrin of big businesses.

Blocking the noise made everything faster.

item.itunes:title: I ditched my monitor for a 4K 120Hz projector, and it completely changed my setup
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It shouldn't surprise you that I spend a lot of time in front of a screen. Whether it's for my business or my writing, my days tend to run long. A few years ago, I invested in a large 43-inch monitor to maximize the screen real estate. But as large as it is, you can only fit so much on a desk. Plus, it didn't help that the monitor was locked to 60Hz.

I wanted something with the sharpness of a 4K screen, the smoothness of a high refresh-rate panel, and the ability to go a bit higher for games and movies when I felt like it. A projector seemed like a good fit, except that until very recently, such a projector didn't really exist. Not within a reasonable budget anyway.

However, Texas Instruments recently introduced its DLP472TP chip, which has allowed a range of manufacturers to release 4K/120Hz projectors at less-than-nosebleed prices. I decided to try the JMGO Iris Ultra Max. This 4K projector supports 120Hz output, turning any wall into a screen larger than any monitor has any right to be, but it's the other bells and whistles that convinced me it's the one.

A projector gives you much more flexibility than a conventional monitor

The motorized gimbal makes switching from work to play effortless

The problem with a conventional monitor is that it effectively becomes the centerpiece of your desk setup. You've got a fixed viewing distance and need to attach a monitor arm or VESA mount, too. I multitask a lot, and my desktop tends to be a clutter of windows, but there's only so big I can go with a monitor.

The JMGO Iris Ultra Max, but for that matter, any projector, lets you scale up and down the screen size depending on what you're doing. What stood out to me about this projector is its optical zoom function. Got a small desk? You can scale down to a smaller, just-as-sharp screen. Need to turn that same projector into a gaming machine? Use the optical zoom to adjust the screen size. I've gone as large as a 120-inch screen, and the results have been tack-sharp.

Even before we get to picture quality and the other specs that made me choose this model, one feature stood out. It's got a built-in motorized gimbal. That means when I'm done with work, I can flip it around and project a massive display on the wall behind me to catch up on Netflix. In fact, the projector can even remember the exact horizon adjustments you made for specific areas. It literally takes seconds to switch spots, making for a brilliant quality-of-life addition.

4K resolution and 120Hz make the projector a viable monitor replacement

The dual iris system helps improve contrast

Of course, size was just one reason I was keen to switch to this model as a monitor. The resolution matters a lot. Given the sheer number of high-density text documents I tend to have on my screen, a 4K setup was a non-negotiable for me.

Just as important was brightness. My work setup sits right by a large window, so I need something that can deliver a usable image in ambient light. Rated at 6500 lumens, the Iris Ultra Max should be more than capable on paper. Realistically, it is, with a small caveat. I found that the rated peak brightness applies only under specific settings, like a pure white screen. The actual brightness is noticeably lower, but not enough to be an issue. If you're using a projector as a monitor, keep in mind that ambient light will affect perceived contrast, and you'll just have to get used to it.

That said, let's talk 120Hz, because it's one of the rarer features around. The projector also has HDMI 2.1 and variable refresh rate support, plus automatic low-latency features. I paired the projector with my MacBook Pro and easily mirrored my laptop's screen at 120Hz. No surprises there.

Part of the reason JMGO has been able to drive down the cost of a 4K, 120Hz projector is that it doesn't actually use a native 4K imaging chip. Instead, it uses a 1080p DLP chip and pairs it with pixel shifting to produce a 4K image. Dual display controllers and a high-speed actuator enable this. While pixel shifting isn't exactly new, it uses two of the aforementioned TI DLP chips to drive the imaging system fast enough to achieve 4K at 120Hz. It's also why the image looks sharp, practically the same as native 4K versus the softer visuals you'd expect from an interpolated or upscaled image.

There's a lot to like here, including built-in Google TV support, which lets me turn the projector into an entertainment system whenever I want. But what stands out most to me is the native contrast ratio achieved via a dual-iris arrangement. This is genuinely cool, as it lets me improve contrast levels in a room with ambient light by physically adjusting the projector's iris. While the projector works best with an ALR screen to eke out the best possible image quality, I can't fit one in my study. That's where the Iris adjustment has been useful, as I can extract better contrast even when running the projector on a blank white wall.

A more flexible way to work

For now, I've been using the projector straight up on my wall, blowing up a 120Hz screen with my MacBook. Whether I'm writing or editing video, it's been a wonderful experience. Look, this isn't a replacement for hardcore monitor nerds or even gamers. Casual gamers and entertainment enthusiasts will find the JMGO Ultra Max more than satisfactory, and it does a fantastic job even if all you're looking for is a way to maximize screen real estate.

It isn't perfect, and brightness levels aren't quite what the marketing claims, but that's a problem that plagues practically every projector on the market. What completes the package is what the projector offers beyond that. Whether it's the sharpness of 4K resolution, genuine 120Hz support, or the ability to turn it into an entertainment center on a dime, these are what make it interesting.

For my setup, that's a big plus since I'm not just getting a bigger screen for work, but also the ability to turn it into an entertainment center once I'm done. It's a pricey upgrade over my old monitor, but I can't say anyone would regret making it.

JMGO Iris Ultra Max

item.title: The 3-2-1 backup rule has a glaring caveat that ransomware exploits perfectly
item.itunes:title: The 3-2-1 backup rule has a glaring caveat that ransomware exploits perfectly
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Just about everyone should know about the 3-2-1 backup rule by now. If you don't, it's a strategy that says you should have three copies of your files on two different types of media, with one off-site. Only then are your files truly protected from disasters — or, as I learned recently, most disasters.

See, there's an important caveat to this strategy that people don't talk about enough. Even with three copies of your important files, geographic separation, and snapshots configured, ransomware (or similar malicious software) can take out the main copy and all the backups at once. Fortunately, there's a cheap and straightforward way to deal with this problem: a cold storage backup.

My NAS backup strategy costs $0 a month, and it's more reliable than any cloud service I've tested

It's pretty easy to set up, too

25
By  Ayush Pande

Backups shouldn't be constantly mounted

Malware can spread across all of them

I realized the gap in my backup implementation when I read about ransomware that specifically targets NAS systems. Instead of touching only the files on the main drive, much ransomware will spread across other mounted storage, including backup drives and SMB shares, and encrypt files there too. The only way for a backup to save you in this scenario is if it's detached from the computer and inaccessible.

My setup has a backup drive in the same system as my primary storage. I use an rsync script that I run nightly to synchronize the changes from my main storage pool to the other drive. That setup protects me from hardware failure and corrupt files, but if malware finds its way onto the system, it could easily replicate across those extra copies of my files.

An off-site backup strengthens this setup considerably, but only if it's not trivially accessible from the same computer where the rest of the files live. I mounted my offsite backup as a mapped network drive, which was the whole issue. It makes backups easier and allows me to browse files in a more convenient way, but it's a double-edged sword that unintentionally gives anything malicious on my PC a direct gateway to another copy of my files.

The same goes for snapshots and other layers of protection. If they're stored alongside the primary copy of your files, and the device gets hit with ransomware or malware, they'll likely get caught up in the attack as well. My automated backup would've also propagated ransomware to other copies of my files, had I been unfortunate enough to get infected. It's supposed to be a convenient way to sync my files to a remote VPS, but if my main PC becomes infected without me realizing it, the nightly off-site sync will overwrite my good copies with the compromised data.

An air-gapped backup drive is the simple fix

Infections can't threaten your detached storage

The easiest ransomware protection is nothing fancy. I protect my files with an external drive that stays unplugged and disconnected from the rest of the network unless I'm actively syncing file changes to it. It's as simple as plugging it in once a week or so, running a backup (I use an rsync command), and disconnecting it again once the sync is complete. Here's the command I use:

rsync -avhP --delete /mnt/tank/files/ /mnt/external/backup/

Then, I unmount the drive and tuck it away till next week. There's a plethora of other complex solutions and ransomware detection that you can implement, but I find the simplest fix to be the most elegant. Plus, it's a cheap and straightforward fix that anyone can utilize, and it doesn't rely on special technology or software. Cold storage also offers peace of mind because it doesn't rely on carefully configured software to detect malicious activity. Just disconnect it and forget it.

It's so simple that it doesn't need to be perfect

Live files and cold storage aren't always in sync

If I do actually need to resort to restoring my files from the air-gapped device at some point, they'll likely be slightly out of sync with those on my primary storage. For example, if I last backed up to the detached device five days ago, then I go to restore from it, I've lost the last five days of file changes. That's a fairly small trade-off, all things considered. If every copy of my files has been compromised except for the external drive, I'm not too worried about a few days' worth of changes.

As of now, I haven't been infected by ransomware or anything similar yet. I take the usual precautions online, so the chance of anything happening is relatively small. The external drive gives me enough protection that in the unlikely event something does happen, the slight gap in file sync is an acceptable drawback. I could always back up more frequently if I was worried about the incremental file changes falling too far behind.

Have a copy that nothing else can reach

If you're following the 3-2-1 backup strategy (you should be), but haven't accounted for a ransomware attack, an external drive is the simplest solution that you can start using today. It takes almost no time to set up, and it ensures you always have an extra copy of your files in a desk drawer, in case anything knocks out every other copy.

See, there's an important caveat to this strategy that people don't talk about enough. Even with three copies of your important files, geographic separation, and snapshots configured, ransomware (or similar malicious software) can take out the main copy and all the backups at once. Fortunately, there's a cheap and straightforward way to deal with this problem: a cold storage backup.

My NAS backup strategy costs $0 a month, and it's more reliable than any cloud service I've tested

It's pretty easy to set up, too

25
By  Ayush Pande

Backups shouldn't be constantly mounted

Malware can spread across all of them

I realized the gap in my backup implementation when I read about ransomware that specifically targets NAS systems. Instead of touching only the files on the main drive, much ransomware will spread across other mounted storage, including backup drives and SMB shares, and encrypt files there too. The only way for a backup to save you in this scenario is if it's detached from the computer and inaccessible.

My setup has a backup drive in the same system as my primary storage. I use an rsync script that I run nightly to synchronize the changes from my main storage pool to the other drive. That setup protects me from hardware failure and corrupt files, but if malware finds its way onto the system, it could easily replicate across those extra copies of my files.

An off-site backup strengthens this setup considerably, but only if it's not trivially accessible from the same computer where the rest of the files live. I mounted my offsite backup as a mapped network drive, which was the whole issue. It makes backups easier and allows me to browse files in a more convenient way, but it's a double-edged sword that unintentionally gives anything malicious on my PC a direct gateway to another copy of my files.

The same goes for snapshots and other layers of protection. If they're stored alongside the primary copy of your files, and the device gets hit with ransomware or malware, they'll likely get caught up in the attack as well. My automated backup would've also propagated ransomware to other copies of my files, had I been unfortunate enough to get infected. It's supposed to be a convenient way to sync my files to a remote VPS, but if my main PC becomes infected without me realizing it, the nightly off-site sync will overwrite my good copies with the compromised data.

An air-gapped backup drive is the simple fix

Infections can't threaten your detached storage

The easiest ransomware protection is nothing fancy. I protect my files with an external drive that stays unplugged and disconnected from the rest of the network unless I'm actively syncing file changes to it. It's as simple as plugging it in once a week or so, running a backup (I use an rsync command), and disconnecting it again once the sync is complete. Here's the command I use:

rsync -avhP --delete /mnt/tank/files/ /mnt/external/backup/

Then, I unmount the drive and tuck it away till next week. There's a plethora of other complex solutions and ransomware detection that you can implement, but I find the simplest fix to be the most elegant. Plus, it's a cheap and straightforward fix that anyone can utilize, and it doesn't rely on special technology or software. Cold storage also offers peace of mind because it doesn't rely on carefully configured software to detect malicious activity. Just disconnect it and forget it.

It's so simple that it doesn't need to be perfect

Live files and cold storage aren't always in sync

If I do actually need to resort to restoring my files from the air-gapped device at some point, they'll likely be slightly out of sync with those on my primary storage. For example, if I last backed up to the detached device five days ago, then I go to restore from it, I've lost the last five days of file changes. That's a fairly small trade-off, all things considered. If every copy of my files has been compromised except for the external drive, I'm not too worried about a few days' worth of changes.

As of now, I haven't been infected by ransomware or anything similar yet. I take the usual precautions online, so the chance of anything happening is relatively small. The external drive gives me enough protection that in the unlikely event something does happen, the slight gap in file sync is an acceptable drawback. I could always back up more frequently if I was worried about the incremental file changes falling too far behind.

Have a copy that nothing else can reach

If you're following the 3-2-1 backup strategy (you should be), but haven't accounted for a ransomware attack, an external drive is the simplest solution that you can start using today. It takes almost no time to set up, and it ensures you always have an extra copy of your files in a desk drawer, in case anything knocks out every other copy.

item.title: VitaWave turned my PS Vita into a dedicated music player, and it’s my favorite way to listen to my library
item.itunes:title: VitaWave turned my PS Vita into a dedicated music player, and it’s my favorite way to listen to my library
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Using my PS Vita for media beyond gaming came naturally, mostly because of the amazing homebrew community. I tried Swiftfin to stream content from my Jellyfin server, but one aspect was still missing: music.

While sifting through the homebrew projects, I stumbled upon VitaWave, an open-source music player built from the ground up for the handheld. Once I set it up on my PS Vita, it quietly became my go-to way to listen to music on my gaming handheld.

VitaWave isn't trying to be a Jellyfin client

A dedicated offline player for local music files

Straight up, VitaWave doesn't talk to Jellyfin, or any media server, at least not yet. It's a native homebrew app written in C that reads audio files from the Vita's storage. So whatever I drop into the music folder on my memory card, the player picks it up easily.

VitaWave handles MP3, FLAC, and OGG Vorbis natively, which covers most of my library. I barely need to convert files specifically for it. Honestly, I like the local-only approach to listening to music instead of relying on a network connection or another streaming service. The idea is to listen to music that lives on the Vita to ensure smooth playback and no connectivity issues.

For a dedicated music player, I traded streaming from an online service or a local server for manual file syncing, and the trade was worth it.

Nintendo will never remake Zelda: A Link to the Past in HD-2D, so a fan is doing it instead

The project is in the very early stages, but it's still very impressive

6
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Getting your library onto Vita takes one FTP transfer

VitaWave takes over after VitaShell handles the sync

Installing VitaWave on the PS Vita is as straightforward as installing any other homebrew app. After you grab the latest VPK and install it through VitaShell, it's ready to use. But first, I needed to move a bunch of audio files, FLACs, to the Vita's memory card using VitaShell's built-in FTP server. I used FileZilla on my Mac, connected to VitaShell's FTP server details, and copied the FLAC files from my Jellyfin server's music library into the ux0:music folder on the memory card.

One thing I noticed was that copying files with backslashes or special characters in their names caused an error. So I renamed a few, and then the transfer went smoothly. After the files transfer to the card, each one appears locally in the app. Also, there are no Wi-Fi setting quirks or server lookups needed during playback.

The sound quality features are what sold me

FLAC support and a real equalizer made it my go-to music app

What really made VitaWave different was its support for FLAC files, which lets me enjoy lossless music directly from the Vita's storage. Those lossless files actually sound good, without any compromises along the way. Plus, it has a proper ten-band equalizer with presets I can save myself. That's more control than I'd expect from a homebrew project.

Adjusting sliders or picking presets makes it easy to customize the listening experience. The app also has a built-in spectrum visualizer with bar and waveform modes. The interface looks fresh, with button shortcuts at the bottom of the screen for quick access to shuffle, repeat, and crossfade between tracks.

I can also create playlists and save them as standard M3U files. However, naming one still remains the classic pain of multi-tapping letters on the Vita without any on-screen keyboard. What really takes the cake is that the music app can run in the background while you browse the Vita's interface or lock the screen.

This homebrew app still has a few quirks to live with

No local server sync and manual copying efforts required

VitaWave has become my go-to music player on the Vita, though I do wish it had a few more features. For starters, it doesn't connect to an FTP source directly or sync with my Jellyfin server. So it considers only the files in the music folder as its library. Although transferring music over FTP isn't exactly fast, I'd welcome a quicker option.

It's a homebrew project by a single developer, so it feels a bit rough around the edges compared with a polished commercial app. That said, I haven't run into stability issues, but it's clearly maintained by one person in their spare time. Still, I'd appreciate faster transfer options and support to sync directly with an FTP source or a media server.

My gaming handheld runs my home media server, and it costs nothing to keep running

Gaming handhelds can do more than play games.

By  Abid Ahsan Shanto

Turning my Vita into a dedicated music player

I didn't exactly set out to sync files with my Vita just to listen to music. However, VitaWave made that extra step of putting songs on my console worth it. When I am not gaming or watching anything, playing music turns the console into a neat desk gadget. Plus, real FLAC support and a ten-band equalizer that lets you tune the listening experience really take the setup up a notch.

If you have a modded Vita, try VitaWave to listen to your music library. That extra effort takes less than five minutes to turn your Vita into a music player.

VitaWave

VitaWave is a free, open-source homebrew music player app built ground up for PS Vita. 

See at VitaWave on GitHub

item.title: Google Gemini Notebook now gives you a ton more input over Slide Deck and Video Overview creation
item.itunes:title: Google Gemini Notebook now gives you a ton more input over Slide Deck and Video Overview creation
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Gemini Notebooks now pause and ask for direction when creating slide decks and video overviews.
  • It suggests topics from your sources and lets you choose which points the assets explore.
  • Review toggle lets you tweak outlines or producer notes before rendering, or disable it for hands-off use.

After using AI for a little while, I've come to realise that handing an LLM a task and telling it to "Just get it done" is ripe for disaster. It's always good to have a little bit of a personal touch so the result is just how you like it. As it turns out, people using Google Gemini's Notebook feature have noticed that they have very little control over generating Slide Decks and Video Overviews. Now, Google has added additional customization to Notebooks, where Gemini will pause and ask you the best way to proceed.

Google Gemini Notebooks' Slide Decks and Video Overviews get a bit of a human touch

Now you have a bit more input on how things pan out

As announced on the Google Blog, Gemini Notebooks are letting you steer the output for Slide Decks and Video Overviews. Beforehand, you would sic Gemini on it, and it would generate a result for you without much input; now, it will suggest topics based on your sources and let you pick where you want the assets to explore. The video above shows Gemini presenting the user with a questionnaire before generation, allowing the user to direct the flow better.

There's even a new Review toggle if you want to get granular with it:

"If you want to have even more creative control, you can use our new Review toggle. With this on, you can review the plan in the studio panel by clicking “Review outline notes” for slides and "Review producer notes” for video, plus give additional feedback, like asking to include an executive summary at the beginning or swapping the order of a scene, before anything renders."

Of course, if you know exactly what you want, you can disable this toggle and tell Gemini your requirements. It'll then work away without disturbing you any further. Still, it's good to see new ways to guide the LLM when it's making your content; it saves a lot of headache from prompting and re-prompting until it does what you want it to do.

Gemini just got a new notebooks feature that syncs with NotebookLM

It's a productivity-empowering partnership.

By  Simon Batt

item.title: Self-hosting doesn't actually save you money, and the people who promise it does are setting beginners up to quit
item.itunes:title: Self-hosting doesn't actually save you money, and the people who promise it does are setting beginners up to quit
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I run a Proxmox server with mirrored enterprise drives, a retired RTX 3080, and more containers than I’d like to admit, and I’d recommend self-hosting to almost anyone who’s curious. What I wouldn’t do is promise them it’ll save money, but a lot of home lab enthusiasts lead with that. It is everywhere in beginner guides, and for most people it doesn’t hold up once you take into account drives, backups, electricity, and time. Worse, it sets newcomers up to quit the first time they realize it's not worth it in terms of the dollars saved.

5 things I wish I knew before going all-in on self-hosting

Hosting your own services isn't all fun and games

4
By  Ayush Pande

The hardware math doesn't beat the subscription

With a proper setup, you're probably saving very little

You can start self-hosting with nothing but a cheap mini PC, and it's true that a lot of containers don't require much compute at all, but storage is where the math starts to slip. If you care about the photos you’re moving off Google, you want redundancy, and a ZFS mirror or RAID 1 means buying two drives to get one drive’s worth of space. But then you have to consider that redundancy isn’t a backup, so you set up a proper 3-2-1 setup (three copies, two kinds of media, one offsite) that adds at least one more drive on top of that. Then, you add a UPS so a power flicker doesn’t take the pool down mid-write, and the hardware budget has doubled in the span of a few short months.

Then there’s electricity, which a subscription never bills you for. My own server shows how this adds up. It’s an older i7-6700K build with two mirrored 8TB enterprise SAS drives, an LSI HBA, and an RTX 3080 retired from gaming. I don't have a wall meter to measure exactly how much I'm spending, but I’d estimate it draws somewhere around 100 watts on an average day. Running around the clock, that’s close to 900kWh a year, which in my neck of the woods works out to roughly the price of a streaming subscription every month just to keep it powered. None of that hardware lasts forever, either. Drives wear out, and the box you build today won’t be the one you’re running in five years.

5 things I learned from merging my entire digital life into one self-hosted home lab

Complete control over your data comes with its challenges.

5
By  Sumukh Rao

The costs nobody puts into a spreadsheet

They're not "hidden", but they're not the ones you think of first

Some costs don’t show up until you’re already committed, and remote access is a common one. Plenty of ISPs put customers behind carrier-grade NAT, which rules out simple port forwarding, so you end up relying on a tunnel or mesh VPN service. The free tiers cover a lot of people, but if you’d rather own that piece too, as I do with a self-hosted NetBird control plane, you’re renting a VPS to run it. Most reverse proxy guides also assume you’ve bought a domain, which is another added cost.

Then there's the cost of offsite backups, which, if you're lucky enough to have ownership of more than one physical location, could be as simple as storing a drive there that you routinely backup over the network. For most people, though, an offsite backup means a monthly storage subscription.

The cost that dwarfs all of these is time. Updates break things, containers need migrating, and certificate renewals fail at the worst possible moment. When your photo backup stops working, there’s no support line to call. You are the support line, and that can be the biggest cost of all.

5 things I learned after building my first home lab

There's more to home labs than meets the eye

3
By  Ayush Pande

Selling it as savings is how you lose beginners completely

It's much more useful to look at it from a different perspective

If you completely remove subscriptions and only take into account the static costs of self-hosting, it can eventually pay for itself. It's possible, but getting into it with that intention is probably getting into it for the wrong reasons.

The best reasons to get into self-hosting are the control it affords you, as well as the learning opportunity. Control means your photos live on drives you can touch, and no company can raise the price, shrink your storage tier, or decide that a feature you rely on is now a paid add-on. Learning pays off in knowing your way around Linux, networking, storage, and overall troubleshooting a lot better, and those skills can carry over to almost everything else you do with a computer.

I switched from streaming to self-hosting my media — it cost more than I expected

Trading a recurring cost for an upfront sticker price

38
By  Chandraveer Mathur

There are cases where it can save you money, it's just not the best reason to start

item.title: The file sync app I forget exists has moved my files across four devices for a year
item.itunes:title: The file sync app I forget exists has moved my files across four devices for a year
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The best software is the kind that you can set up once and forget about. One of the best examples I have is Syncthing. I installed it on a few of my devices about a year ago and haven't needed to reconfigure it since the initial setup. I'm still using it every day; I just don't open it.

There are plenty of options for file sync software. Some of the most popular choices are Google Drive, OneDrive, and Dropbox. And they work fine. I've used them. But inevitably, there's always something to tweak or troubleshoot. Syncthing has been less maintenance for me (zero, actually), which is the biggest selling point for any piece of software.

I replaced Dropbox with Syncthing, and file sync finally stopped feeling like I was borrowing someone else’s computer

Syncthing finally gave me file sync without the cloud vendor lock-in

2
By  Ayush Pande

Syncthing keeps files in sync across devices

With no cloud account required

You can't quite compare Syncthing to cloud services because the core model is different. Syncthing is peer-to-peer software, meaning devices talk directly to each other rather than through a company's centralized cloud. There are pros and cons to that approach. On the one hand, you don't need a cloud account or pay a subscription fee. On the other hand, you're in charge of every device, so it's your job to make sure that all systems are reachable and that your files are backed up.

Setup is pretty painless because Syncthing handles most of it. On my LAN, devices found each other instantly without any manual configuration. For devices that aren't on the same network, Syncthing uses relay servers to connect them. All file transfers are still encrypted end-to-end, so there's no risk of those servers snooping on any of your files.

When a file changes, Syncthing only sends the updated blocks of it to the other devices that it's set to synchronize with. It uses the same delta-transfer method that rsync employs, which is what makes it so fast. In other words, appending new data to a large file won't spark a re-transfer of the whole file — only the changed data.

I have four devices sharing data with each other

They all have the same files, all the time

For my setup, Syncthing runs on four different devices, and keeps a single folder in sync between them. That includes my Windows desktop, Windows laptop, a NAS server running Ubuntu, and an HTPC hooked up to my TV. The folder is configured as receive-only on the HTPC, meaning that it can't write changes to the shared folder. On the other three devices, you can read data from the shared folder, but you can also add new files. I just don't need the two-way transfers on the HTPC, since all it usually does is play video files.

One of the reasons I never think about Syncthing is because it just runs as a background service on all my systems. On Windows, I know it's running because I can see the icon in my taskbar. My Ubuntu server doesn't have a GUI, but it automatically starts the relevant systemd service on boot. I don't need to manually start the background service or open the app unless I need to configure something. My setup is pretty straightforward with only one shared folder, so I haven't needed to make any changes.

The only hiccups (if I can even call them that) I've encountered are when an offline device changes a file, and those changes conflict with another copy when it finally syncs. That has happened a handful of times over the past year, but Syncthing handles it pretty well. Rather than picking only one winner and overwriting the other file, it'll save both of them, with one copy bearing a .sync-conflict file extension. If that happens, I check out both files, decide which one to keep, and get rid of the other. It's an elegant way to ensure you don't lose either file, and so far I haven't.

Cloud storage still has two nice features

But I wouldn't necessarily call them "advantages"

A lot of people reach for cloud storage out of convenience alone. The fact that it can keep a shared folder in sync across several devices is sort of a byproduct of its main service, which is to store files in the cloud. It can be handy to have another copy of files in the cloud, but I'd rather opt out of that and just keep the syncing function, so Syncthing works better for me. My files are already on four devices anyway, so I don't need them on a company's server for a fifth location.

Cloud providers also offer more user-friendly installation and setup. A better audience for Syncthing is the DIY and home-server crowd. It fits in perfectly with a slew of other open-source, self-hosted services that my home lab runs. That's not to say that it's too complicated for everyday users, though. But the initial setup demands a bit more from you than, say, Dropbox. You need to configure shared folders and permissions, make sure the devices can reach each other (firewalls and NAT rules can get in the way), and you still have the onus of taking regular backups, since file syncing is not a total backup strategy by itself. After the first-time setup, it's a breeze.

Apps I forget about are the best

My favorite thing about Syncthing is that I don't ever need to interact with it directly. It silently does its job in the background, keeping a folder synchronized across various devices, and I don't need to do anything extra. If you're looking for a seamless way to transfer files between your devices, Syncthing is worth setting up.
